proposals.proposal: Inspect the daily-blog-post workflow file for the root cause of the failure at 04:02 UTC. The most common causes in Astro-based CI pipelines are: a Node version mismatch after a runner image update, an expired API key used to call the content-generation step, or a changed output path that the workflow's artifact-upload step no longer resolves. Pull the raw logs from run sha bf0ec8b's sibling run, identify the failing step, and patch only that step. Do not touch the workflow trigger schedule or the funnel-hack job in the same file pass — keep the diff minimal. Once the blog workflow passes, the queue will refill and organic traffic signals can be read cleanly again.

proposals.observation: The Money Vigilance automation has the strongest open rate of the three active sequences: 66.67% on 12 sends. Money Avoidance sits at 52.63% and Money Worship at 37.5%. The vigilance audience, people who watch, restrict, and quietly brace against money rather than avoiding or worshipping it, is the most intellectually engaged segment Joel works with. That 66% figure says the subject line already has purchase, but there is room to push it toward 70%+ by making the subject line more forensically specific to the vigilance experience, so it reads as recognition rather than description.
proposals.proposal: Replace the opening subject line in the Money Vigilance sequence with one that names the specific internal experience of a vigilance reader rather than labelling the pattern from the outside. The current subject describes the behaviour. proposals.new_text:
---
title: "Why do I keep the pension tab open for weeks and never actually click into it?"
pubDate: "2026-08-29"
description: "The tab sits there. You know it does. Here is what that waiting is actually about."
---

You have had the tab open since Tuesday.

Not this Tuesday. The one before.

It is the pension provider login page, or the HMRC self-assessment start screen, or the savings account you transferred money into eight months ago and have not looked at since. The tab does not close. It does not move. It just sits there at the far right of your browser bar, too small to read the favicon, and every time your eyes catch it you feel a low, specific dread that you immediately redirect somewhere else.

Joel knows that tab. He had a version of it for a long time. Not a browser tab, in his case, but a gym bag that lived by the front door for eleven days, packed and ready, never leaving the flat. The bag was not laziness. The bag was a very organised way of not having to decide whether he was the kind of person who goes to the gym now. The tab works the same way. As long as it is open, you are technically still intending to deal with it.

This is not a discipline problem. It is not a willpower problem.

It is what happens when looking at the number feels like a verdict on you rather than information about your money.

The avoidance is not the thing you need to fix. It is a signal pointing at something underneath: a belief, usually quiet and usually old, that whatever the number says will confirm something you are already afraid is true.

The work is not opening the tab.

The work is getting curious about what you think will happen if you do.

Joel is a Qualified Financial Planner with an MSc in Behavioural Economics. He works with people in their 20s and 30s who earn well and still find themselves standing next to a packed gym bag wondering why they cannot just go.

If that sentence landed somewhere specific in your chest, [the free money-type quiz](#) takes four minutes and tells you exactly which pattern is running the show.
